newsitem.title: UK: Jochimsen warns of EMU "coalition of sinners".
newsitem.headline: Jochimsen warns of EMU "coalition of sinners".

text.p: The drive among European nations to join a single currency is making "budgetary fudging" the order of the day and risks a "coalition of sinners" said Reimut Jochimsen, a policy-making member of Germany's Bundesbank.

In an article he wrote for The European newspaper, to be published on Thursday, Jochimsen said attempts to create "problem-solving councils and pacts" contravened the Maastricht Treaty of 1993, which set the timetable and criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

"The same lack of trust is generated by the ease with which budgetary fudging has become the order of the day to fulfil formally the criteria of the Maastricht Treaty," he wrote the day after a row broke out over Italy's plans to join EMU from the start in 1999.
To qualify for EMU, nations must meet tough standards for inflation, debt, deficits, interest rates and exchange rates.

European Union nations held a summit in Dublin last December and agreed on a stability pact, which insists that EMU members must continue to keep annual budget deficits at three percent of their GDP or below after monetary union or risk being fined.
Jochimsen said that at the Dublin summit there had been a growing understanding that a stable European currency, the euro, needed solid, sustainable public finances in all member states.
"But that's too good to be true, because upon closer scrutiny the stability pact still lacks substance," he said.
The pact did not contain proposed sanctions against countries running deficits or any rule that required such countries to prove why they should be exempt from fines, Jochimsen said.
An ineffective stability pact meant the Maastricht Treaty's conditions for EMU entry risked losing effect, he said.
"Already there is talk of determining violations of the stability agreement 'on a case-by-case basis'," he said.
Anybody seeking this way of solving problems might swiftly have to deal with a "coalition of sinners" which might lead to a weak and unstable euro and, in effect, a strong dollar.
"The final act -- the abolition of Europe's anchor currency, the deutschemark, in exchange for a weak common one -- could turn out to be a dubious contribution to EU integration," he wrote.
"There is not yet enough trust and confidence to make the new euro a stable and strong currency as intended by the treaty."
